analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal pipeline safety enforcement while adding procedural limits that slow new regulation of pipeline operators.
analysis.headline: The House passed it by voice vote and the Senate passed it without objection, and it was signed into law as Public Law 112-90 on January 3, 2012.
analysis.plain_summary: This law raises the fines pipeline companies can face for safety violations (the maximum per violation doubles to $200,000 and the maximum for a series of violations doubles to $2,000,000), lets the Transportation Department penalize companies that obstruct investigations, requires automatic or remote-controlled shutoff valves on new transmission pipelines, forces operators to verify their records and pressure-test older gas pipelines in populated areas, and funds state safety programs through 2015. At the same time, it blocks the regulator from issuing several major new safety rules until studies are done and Congress has had a review period, and it leaves oil production flow lines and most gathering lines unregulated.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live or work near pipelines, especially in designated high-consequence areas, get stronger enforcement, faster accident reporting (notice within one hour of confirmed discovery), required pressure testing of previously untested gas lines, and better information for emergency responders. State safety programs get federal grants and hardship waivers, and states lose grant eligibility if they exempt their own agencies from one-call digging-notification rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near pipelines and state safety agencies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the maximum civil penalty to $200,000 per violation and $2,000,000 for a related series of violations, removes the cap on administrative enforcement penalties, and lets regulators fine operators who obstruct inspections or investigations.

Requires the Secretary of Transportation to mandate automatic or remote-controlled shutoff valves on new or entirely replaced transmission pipelines where feasible, and requires record verification and material-strength testing rules for previously untested natural gas transmission pipelines in high-consequence areas.
Requires operators to notify regulators and the National Response Center within one hour of a confirmed accident, and to update release estimates within 48 hours.

Authorizes pipeline safety grants, emergency response grants, one-call notification programs, and state damage prevention program funding for fiscal years 2012 through 2015, and lets states economically harmed get waivers from matching-fund requirements.
Conditions state grant eligibility on not exempting municipalities, state agencies, or their contractors from one-call excavation-notification requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators, who face higher fines, mandatory record verification and pressure testing, design-review fees for very large projects, and new equipment requirements; these costs are commonly recovered through shipping charges and utility rates over time.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pipeline operators and eventually energy customers

drawbacks.text: The Secretary of Transportation may not issue final rules requiring leak detection systems, or expanding integrity management requirements beyond high-consequence areas, until study reports are complete and a congressional review period ends, and then only if the Secretary makes specific findings — so the two most sweeping potential safety mandates are studied first and delayed.

The law expressly does not authorize the Secretary to set standards for oil production flow lines on well grounds or production facilities, and leaves most onshore and offshore gathering lines unregulated pending a two-year review with only optional follow-on regulation.

Key requirements are qualified: shutoff valves and excess flow valves are required only 'where economically, technically, and operationally feasible' and 'if appropriate', and pressure-testing timeframes must minimize costs and service disruptions, which gives the regulator and industry room to phase in or narrow the mandates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real, enforceable safety gains — doubled penalties, mandatory shutoff valves on new lines, pressure testing of old gas lines, one-hour accident reporting, and grant funding — in exchange for costs to operators that are modest relative to the sector's size. The honest trade-off is on the regulatory side: the same law that strengthens enforcement also defers the broadest new mandates (leak detection standards, integrity management beyond high-consequence areas) behind studies and review periods, and preserves exemptions for gathering lines and production flow lines. It is a stronger-than-status-quo law that stops short of the more expansive regulation it contemplates.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it under a fast-track procedure with a voice vote, the Senate passed it unchanged by unanimous consent a day later, and the president signed it on January 3, 2012.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 7, 2011 and its subcommittee was discharged the next day; the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee marked it up on September 8 and ordered it reported as amended by voice vote.
The committee reported it amended on December 1, 2011 (H. Rept. 112-297), the Energy and Commerce Committee was discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
On December 12, 2011 the House passed it under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills — by voice vote, so no individual votes were recorded.
The Senate received the bill on December 13, 2011 and passed it without amendment by unanimous consent, so no individual votes were recorded there either.
It was presented to the president on December 23, 2011 and signed on January 3, 2012, becoming Public Law 112-90.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People living near pipelines gained enforceable safety upgrades, and pipeline operators also came out ahead relative to stricter alternatives: the most sweeping potential mandates were converted into study-and-review processes, and gathering-line and flow-line exemptions survived.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near pipelines, plus pipeline operators

sides.party_line_note: There is no recorded opposition anywhere in the action history: the House voice vote, the Senate's unanimous consent, and the lone cosponsor (a Republican joining the Republican sponsor) all point to a noncontroversial, bipartisan bill that moved in roughly three months from introduction to the president's desk.

industries.note: They face doubled fines, mandatory record verification and pressure testing, and new shutoff valve requirements on new or replaced lines, but they also gained procedural delays on leak detection and integrity-management expansion and kept gathering lines and production flow lines outside federal standards.

industries.industry: Large pipeline construction projects (gas, LNG, and hazardous liquid sponsors)
industries.note: Sponsors of projects costing $2.5 billion or more, or using novel designs, must pay the government's costs for design safety reviews and submit plans 120 days before construction.

industries.industry: State pipeline safety programs and emergency responders
industries.note: Grants, training, pipeline mapping tools, and one-hour accident notification requirements give state and local responders better information; states must end exemptions for their own agencies to keep grant eligibility.

They may be required to install excess flow valves on multifamily and small commercial services where feasible, and must consider seismic threats, but the valve mandate applies only if the Secretary finds it appropriate.
